The ballroom emptied faster than any charity dinner in Sterling Hotel history.

William ordered security to close the private executive floor and escorted Anna away from the guests.

Victoria attempted to follow.

William stopped her at the elevator.

“No.”

“You’re making a mistake.”

“You assaulted an employee.”

“She isn’t what you think.”

William pressed the elevator button.

“What do I think?”

Victoria looked at Anna.

Hatred was still there.

But beneath it was something much more revealing.

Recognition.

“You think she arrived here by accident.”

Anna stepped forward.

“I applied for this job six months ago.”

Victoria laughed once.

“You really believe that?”

William moved between them.

“Leave.”

Victoria’s expression hardened.

“You always were sentimental.”

The elevator doors closed between them.

William took Anna to his private office overlooking the city.

Neither sat.

Anna still wore the wine-soaked uniform.

She held the broken pendant tightly.

“My mother gave me this when I turned eighteen,” she said. “She told me it belonged to my birth mother.”

William looked up sharply.

“Mary wasn’t your biological mother?”

“No.”

Anna had always known she was adopted.

Mary Miller never hid that.

But she claimed the adoption was private and that Anna’s biological parents had died when she was an infant.

There were no photographs.

No names.

Only the pendant.

Mary refused to explain where it came from.

“She told me never to sell it,” Anna continued. “Even when we needed money.”

William noticed the way she said we.

“What happened to Mary?”

“Cancer. Three years ago.”

“I’m sorry.”

Anna nodded.

She had worked two jobs during Mary’s illness.

Most of what little they owned disappeared into medical bills.

After Mary died, Anna moved into a small apartment and eventually took the housekeeping position at the Grand Sterling because it included health insurance and steady hours.

William walked toward the window.

“On June seventeenth, 1999, my father brought me to Room 1908.”

Anna stared.

“You remember the date?”

“I remember because it was my mother’s birthday.”

William had been eleven.

The hotel’s nineteenth floor was then partly residential. His family maintained several private suites above the public guest floors.

His father, Charles Sterling, woke him after midnight and took him upstairs.

There was a woman crying in the bedroom.

William never saw her face clearly.

Another woman stood beside the door.

His mother, Eleanor.

And on the bed was a newborn girl.

“My father put her in my arms.”

William looked at Anna.

“He told me her name was Anna.”

The room became silent.

Anna’s fingers closed around the pendant.

“What happened to her?”

“I don’t know.”

William remembered his mother pulling Charles into the hallway.

He remembered raised voices.

He remembered hearing his aunt Helena’s name.

Helena Sterling.

Victoria’s mother.

Then Victoria herself appeared in the doorway.

Fifteen years old.

Old enough to understand more than William did.

“She saw the baby?”

“Yes.”

The next morning William asked where Anna was.

His father said there had been complications.

His mother told him the child had not survived.

“No funeral?”

William shook his head.

“No death announcement either.”

Anna’s voice dropped.

“You believed them?”

“I was eleven.”

That answer sounded weak even to him.

William spent years forgetting the night because everyone around him behaved as though it had never happened.

He looked at the note again.

Room 1908.

Anna whispered, “Does that room still exist?”

William hesitated.

The nineteenth floor had been renovated fifteen years ago.

Room numbers changed.

Except one suite.

1908 had been sealed.

William had always assumed structural damage made it unusable.

He called hotel engineering.

The chief engineer answered.

William asked for the current access status of the old room.

The man went silent.

“Sir, that suite isn’t in our active floor plan.”

“I know.”

“I don’t think anyone has opened it in years.”

“Who has the key?”

Another pause.

“Family legal.”

William frowned.

“Meaning?”

“Mr. Conrad Vale’s office.”

Conrad Vale had served as Sterling family attorney for more than thirty years.

Anna noticed William’s expression.

“What?”

William ended the call.

“Someone deliberately kept that room outside hotel control.”

Anna looked toward the broken pendant.

“Then we open it.”

Before William could answer, his phone buzzed.

Security had stopped Victoria in the underground garage.

She had been trying to leave with a box removed from the nineteenth-floor records archive.

William ordered them to hold her.

Then he received a photograph of the box.

Written across the top in faded marker were two words.

Anna Miller.
